reconcile.connective: Commentators note Phoenicia was the same territory anciently called Canaan, so Matthew's "Canaanite" and Mark's "Syrophoenician"/"Greek" name the same woman differently, not two women.

discrepancy.connective: Redaction critics Davies and Allison read Matthew's swap of Mark's contemporary "Syrophoenician" for the archaic "Canaanite" as a deliberate theological rewriting, not a synonym.

skeptic.name: W. D. Davies and Dale C. Allison
skeptic.work: A Critical and Exegetical Commentary on the Gospel According to Saint Matthew, Vol. 2 (ICC)
skeptic.attribution: W. D. Davies and Dale C. Allison, A Critical and Exegetical Commentary on the Gospel According to Saint Matthew, Vol. 2 (ICC; Edinburgh: T&T Clark, 1991), pp. 541-557

excerpts.excerpt_text: That is, of Phoenicia, which was called Canaan … hence this woman is by Mark said to be a Greek, that is, a Gentile, as the Jews used to call all of another nation, and a Syrophenician, being a native of Phoenicia, called Syrophenician; because it bordered upon Syria, and had been formerly a part of it, by conquest …
excerpts.on_tension_rationale: Directly equates Canaan with ancient Phoenicia, explaining why Mark could call the same woman 'Greek'/'Syrophenician' — the core reconciling move.

excerpts.excerpt_text: Of the flock of the Canaanites, which dwelled in Phoenicia.
excerpts.on_tension_rationale: Geneva marginal note glosses 'woman of Canaan' as an inhabitant of Phoenicia, supporting the Canaan=Phoenicia equation Mark's designation depends on.

excerpts.excerpt_text: Literally Canaanite woman. Matthew uses this archaic Old Testament expression to describe the woman as a pagan.
excerpts.on_tension_rationale: Modern study note frames Matthew's 'Canaanite' as a deliberate archaic OT label for 'pagan,' distinguishing it from Mark's contemporary ethnic/regional term rather than treating them as competing factual claims.

pd_work.resource: John W. Haley, An Examination of the Alleged Discrepancies of the Bible (1874), p. 339
pd_work.author: John W. Haley
pd_work.note: Haley treats this exact pairing under a parallel-column heading — "Woman a Canaanite. / A Syro-Phenician." (Matt. xv. 22 / Mark vii. 26) — explaining she lived in the part of Canaan called Syro-Phoenicia and was herself a "Greek," that is, a Gentile, as opposed to a Jew.
